note: Placed at Doboka in the Kopili–Jamuna valley. Its extent is not recorded; the shape is the present Hojai and West Karbi Anglong districts.
Early Kamarupa: the Brahmaputra valley around Pragjyotishpura. No boundary is recorded for the 4th–5th centuries; the Karatoya is the traditional western limit.
Davaka is absorbed and Bhutivarman's grant (6th c.) reaches the Sylhet region, so the kingdom stretches from the Karatoya to the Bharali and south into the Surma valley.
Bhaskaravarman at his height: ally of Harsha, host of Xuanzang (c. 640).

label: Gauda (campaign reach)
note: After Harsha's death Bhaskaravarman issues the Nidhanpur grant from a victory camp at Karnasuvarna. How much of Gauda he held, and for how long, is disputed: this is campaign reach, not a border.
Same core as the Varman kingdom, without firm evidence of the Sylhet grants. Capital at Haruppeswara (Tezpur) under the later kings.
Harjaravarman (c. 815–832) and Vanamalavarmadeva rule to the Dikrong on the north bank; Harjara's Tezpur rock inscription (829) is the best dated record.
Ratnapala and Indrapala issue grants across the valley. The south bank of the Brahmaputra is the core.
The Paschimbhag plate of Srichandra (c. 930) grants land in Srihatta. Later local kings (the Gaur line) are known mainly from tradition.
A patchwork rather than one kingdom: Bengal's governors in the west, a 'lunar dynasty' on the north bank (one inscription of 1185) and kings remembered as Prithu and Sandhya.

label: Western Kamarupa
note: Ramapala's conquest; Timgyadeva and then Vaidyadeva govern it. The eastern limit is a guess.
The founding by Birpal in 1187 is traditional; there are no records for this period.

At its height the kingdom held the north bank from the Subansiri (present Lakhimpur and Dhemaji) to Parshuram Kund; the earlier map data puts the western limit at the Sisi. Inscriptions of Nandi, Satyanarayana and their successors, ruling from Sadhayapura (Sadiya).
Sukaphaa settles the land between the Dikhow and the Patkai, moving between camps before settling at Charaideo (1253).
South of the Brahmaputra, with the Chutias across the river. The Dikhow is the frontier with the Kacharis. Interregnums 1364–1397; Sudangphaa fixes the Patkai boundary in 1401.
Suhungmung annexes the Chutia kingdom (1523) and pushes the Kacharis back to the Dhansiri.
The Kolong in Nagaon becomes the western limit after the Dimasa capital Dimapur is sacked (1536).
Chilarai's Koch army takes Garhgaon (1563). By the Treaty of Majuli the Ahoms keep the land east of Narayanpur on the north bank.
Bordering Koch Hajo at the Bharali (north) and the Kolong (south).
Pratap Singha faces the Mughals; the frontier post is at Kajali.
After the victory at Sualkuchi (1636) the Ahoms hold up to Hajo.
The Treaty of Asurar Ali (1639): the Barnadi on the north bank, Asurar Ali at Guwahati on the south.
Jayadhwaj Singha takes Kamrup during the Mughal war of succession (1658): the greatest extent of the kingdom. The western limit is not named in the sources; the Manas is used here.

label: Mir Jumla's occupation
note: Mir Jumla occupies Garhgaon (March 1662 – January 1663); the Ahom king withdraws to the hills.
The Treaty of Ghilajharighat (1663) cedes the land west of the Bharali and the Kolong.
Guwahati recovered (1667); Lachit Borphukan defeats Ram Singh at Saraighat (1671).
Laluksola Borphukan hands Guwahati to the Mughals (1679) during the turmoil of the 'boy kings'.
Gadadhar Singha's victory at Itakhuli (1682) fixes the Manas as the western frontier for good.
Kings are now made and unmade by Burmese armies (1817, 1819).
From the Karatoya to the Barnadi, with looser control east of the Manas.
Dimapur on the Dhansiri; the Dikhow is the frontier with the Ahoms (Ahom account).
Pushed back to the Dhansiri; Dimapur is sacked by the Ahoms in 1536.
Capital at Maibong. Yasho Narayan (1583–1601) is the strongest king; Rudra Singha's Ahom army takes Maibong in 1706.
The kingdom moves down to the Cachar plains (Khaspur) after absorbing the Koch Khaspur line.

label: Tularam's hill state
note: After the British annex the Cachar plains (1832), Tularam Senapati keeps the North Cachar hills until 1854.
The Bhuyans hold the north bank between Kamata and the Chutias, sometimes as allies of Kamata.
Harup Narayan's Bhuyans throw out the Sultanate's garrison and briefly hold the west.
The Koch take the west and the Ahoms absorb the rest by c. 1530.
Kamatapur's walls and moats (Gosanimari) date from this time.

label: Sylhet
note: Shah Jalal and the Sultanate's army take Sylhet (1303).
Husain Shah's Kamata, held up to Hajo by 1502.
The Jaintia hills and the plains around Jaintiapur. The outline is approximate.
Biswa Singha's kingdom, from the Karatoya to the Barnadi.
Nara Narayan and his brother and general Chilarai. Chilarai's campaigns make the Kacharis, Jaintia, Manipur, Tripura and Sylhet pay tribute (not shown).
The height of the Koch kingdom after the Treaty of Majuli.
The western half, from Cooch Behar. A British protected state from 1773.
Raghudev's eastern half, from the Sankosh to the Bharali.
Founded by Kamal Narayan, Chilarai's brother, as governor of the Cachar plains.

label: Sylhet
note: Sylhet under Mughal Bengal (and from 1717 the Nawabs of Bengal).
Mughal Kamrup after the fall of Koch Hajo, governed from Hajo.
The Treaty of Asurar Ali (1639).
Kamrup and Darrang ceded by the Treaty of Ghilajharighat.
Ram Singh's army fails to retake Guwahati (Saraighat, 1671).
Guwahati is handed over by Laluksola Borphukan (1679).
Goalpara (the land between the Sankosh and the Manas) under Mughal Bengal.
The land between the Brahmaputra and the Burhidihing around Bengmara. The outline uses the present Tinsukia district.
Burmese occupation of the whole valley; Chandrakanta Singha is driven out (1821–1822).
The British take Guwahati (March 1824) and advance up the valley.

label: East India Company
note: The Company receives the Diwani of Bengal (1765), including Goalpara and Sylhet.
The First Anglo-Burmese War: British troops occupy Lower Assam.
Rangpur falls (January 1825) and the Treaty of Yandabo (24 February 1826) cedes Assam.
The Cachar plains are annexed (1832) after the death of Govindachandra.

label: Purandar Singha's Upper Assam
note: The British restore Purandar Singha as a tributary king of Upper Assam (1833) and take it back in 1838.
Jaintia is annexed (1835), Upper Assam (1838) and the Matak and Sadiya tracts (1839).
North Cachar is annexed (1854). Tea gardens spread across the valley; the Garo and Naga hills are brought under control in the 1860s–70s.

label: Province of Assam
note: Assam becomes a Chief Commissioner's province (1874), with Sylhet, Cachar and the Garo, Khasi-Jaintia and Naga hills. Capital: Shillong.

label: Province of Assam
note: The Lushai hills (Mizoram) join the province (1898).

label: Eastern Bengal and Assam
note: The Partition of Bengal joins Assam with eastern Bengal; capital Dacca.

label: Province of Assam
note: The partition is reversed and Assam becomes a province again (1912).

label: Province of Assam
note: The North-East Frontier Tracts (now Arunachal Pradesh) are added after the McMahon Line (1914); much of them is administered only loosely.

label: Assam
note: Independence; Sylhet goes to Pakistan but Karimganj stays. The North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) is administered through the Governor of Assam.

label: Assam
note: The Naga Hills–Tuensang Area is separated (1957) and becomes Nagaland (1963).

label: Assam
note: Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal are separated (21 January 1972); the capital moves from Shillong to Dispur.

label: Sylhet
note: The Sylhet referendum (July 1947).

label: Sylhet
note: The Bangladesh Liberation War (1971).

label: Nagaland
note: Naga Hills–Tuensang Area (1957); state of Nagaland (1963).

label: Meghalaya
note: An autonomous state within Assam from 1970; a full state from 1972.

label: Mizoram
note: A Union Territory from 1972; a state from 1987.

label: Arunachal Pradesh
note: A Union Territory from 1972; a state from 1987.
